title: Layout with Flexbox and Grid
intro: Modern CSS gives you two powerful tools for arranging elements: Flexbox for one-dimensional layouts and Grid for two-dimensional layouts. Once you understand the container, items, axes, and a few core properties, most everyday layouts become much easier to build.
body:
## Why layout used to be hard CSS layout was not always designed around the kinds of interfaces we build today. Developers used techniques such as tables, floats, inline-blocks, absolute positioning, and complicated margin tricks to place things next to each other or align them vertically. These techniques could work, but they often became difficult to maintain. A layout that looked correct at one width could break when text became longer, a new item was added, or the screen became smaller. Flexbox and Grid were created to solve different parts of this problem. They let you describe the relationship between elements instead of manually calculating where every element should go. A useful mental model is: - **Flexbox** arranges items along one direction. - **Grid** arranges items across rows and columns. You will often use both in the same application. --- ## Flexbox: arranging items in one dimension Flexbox starts with a **flex container** and its **flex items**. ~~~diagram {"type": "flow", "title": "Main axis and cross axis", "caption": "justify-content works along the main axis, align-items across it. flex-direction: column swaps them.", "nodes": [{"id": "c", "label": "display: flex", "kind": "code", "highlight": true}, {"id": "m", "label": "Main axis", "sub": "row → left to right"}, {"id": "x", "label": "Cross axis", "sub": "top to bottom"}, {"id": "j", "label": "justify-content", "sub": "start · center · space-between"}, {"id": "a", "label": "align-items", "sub": "stretch · center · end"}], "edges": [{"from": "c", "to": "m"}, {"from": "c", "to": "x"}, {"from": "m", "to": "j", "label": "controlled by"}, {"from": "x", "to": "a", "label": "controlled by"}]} ~~~ You make an element a flex container with: ~~~css .container { display: flex; } ~~~ Its direct children automatically become flex items. For example: ~~~html
One
Two
Three
~~~ The three inner elements are now flex items. By default, Flexbox places them next to each other horizontally. The important point is that most Flexbox properties are applied to the **container**, while some properties such as `flex` are applied to the **items**. ### Main axis and cross axis Flexbox has two axes. The **main axis** is the direction in which the items are arranged. The **cross axis** is perpendicular to it. With the default `flex-direction: row`, the main axis is horizontal and the cross axis is vertical. ~~~text Main axis → → → [ One ] [ Two ] [ Three ] ↑ │ Cross axis ↓ ~~~ If you change the direction to `column`, the axes change as well: ~~~css .container { display: flex; flex-direction: column; } ~~~ Now the main axis is vertical. ### flex-direction The most common values are `row` and `column`. ~~~css .row { display: flex; flex-direction: row; } .column { display: flex; flex-direction: column; } ~~~ There are also `row-reverse` and `column-reverse`, although you should use them carefully because changing visual order can create accessibility and usability problems. ### justify-content `justify-content` controls how items are distributed along the **main axis**. Common values include: ~~~css .container { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; } ~~~ Useful values are: - `flex-start` — items start at the beginning. - `center` — items are grouped in the center. - `flex-end` — items move to the end. - `space-between` — equal space is placed between items. - `space-around` — space is placed around items. - `space-evenly` — equal space is placed between and around items. A classic navigation bar might use `space-between` to keep a logo on the left and navigation links on the right. ~~~css header { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; } ~~~ ### align-items `align-items` controls how items are aligned along the **cross axis**. For a horizontal row, this normally means vertical alignment. ~~~css header { display: flex; align-items: center; } ~~~ This is one of the most useful CSS rules you will learn. It is often the difference between a button or icon looking slightly too high or low and everything being perfectly aligned. ### gap Instead of giving every item a margin, you can use `gap`. ~~~css .menu { display: flex; gap: 1rem; } ~~~ This creates consistent space between flex items. It also works with Grid. ### flex-wrap By default, flex items try to stay on one line. `flex-wrap` allows them to move onto additional lines. ~~~css .cards { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1rem; } ~~~ This can be useful for a row of cards where the available width is not always known. ### flex: 1 and flex-basis Flex items can share available space using `flex`. ~~~css .card { flex: 1; } ~~~ If several items have `flex: 1`, they will generally share the available space equally, subject to their minimum sizes and other constraints. `flex-basis` controls the initial size of an item before remaining free space is distributed. ~~~css .card { flex: 1 1 240px; } ~~~ This means, roughly, that the item can grow, can shrink, and starts with a basis of `240px`. You do not need to memorize the entire Flexbox algorithm at first. Learn the common patterns and use DevTools when you need to understand a particular layout. --- ## A practical Flexbox example Imagine a simple navigation bar: ~~~html
My Site
About Projects Contact
~~~ The CSS can be very small: ~~~css .site-header { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; padding: 1rem; } .menu { display: flex; gap: 1rem; } ~~~ This is a good example of why Flexbox is useful. You are describing the relationship between the logo and navigation rather than assigning coordinates to each element. --- ## Grid: rows and columns together Flexbox is excellent when the main concern is one direction. Grid is designed for layouts where rows and columns matter at the same time. A Grid container starts with: ~~~css .gallery { display: grid; } ~~~ You can define columns with `grid-template-columns`. ~~~css .gallery { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr; gap: 1rem; } ~~~ This creates three equal columns. ### The fr unit `fr` means a fraction of the available space. For example: ~~~css grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr; ~~~ The first column gets one fraction and the second gets two fractions. Ignoring gaps and other constraints, the second column is approximately twice as wide as the first. You can also use `repeat()` to avoid writing the same value repeatedly. ~~~css grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); ~~~ This means three equal columns. ### Rows Grid can explicitly define rows too: ~~~css grid-template-rows: 80px 1fr 60px; ~~~ This might describe a page with a fixed-height header, flexible main content, and a fixed-height footer. In many card grids, however, you do not need to define rows manually. Grid can create them automatically as items are added. ### minmax() `minmax()` lets you specify a minimum and maximum size. ~~~css grid-template-columns: repeat(3, minmax(180px, 1fr)); ~~~ A column should not become narrower than `180px`, but it can grow to use available space. ### auto-fit for responsive card grids One particularly useful pattern combines `auto-fit`, `minmax()`, and `1fr`: ~~~css .gallery { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr)); gap: 1rem; } ~~~ This tells the browser to fit as many columns as possible while keeping each column at least about `220px` wide. The result can adapt to the available width without writing a media query for every screen size. This is especially useful for product cards, article cards, project cards, and image galleries. --- ## Grid template areas Grid can also describe a page layout using named areas. ~~~css .page { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 220px 1fr; grid-template-areas: "header header" "sidebar main" "footer footer"; } header { grid-area: header; } aside { grid-area: sidebar; } main { grid-area: main; } footer { grid-area: footer; } ~~~ The names make the layout easier to understand because the CSS describes the structure directly. You can think of it as drawing the page with text: ~~~text +---------------------------+ | header | +---------+-----------------+ | sidebar | main | | | | +---------+-----------------+ | footer | +---------------------------+ ~~~ Grid's `gap` property works in the same general way as Flexbox. ~~~css grid { gap: 1rem; } ~~~ You can also use `row-gap` and `column-gap` when the two directions need different spacing. --- ## How do you choose? A simple rule will take you surprisingly far: ~~~widget flex-playground ~~~ ~~~compare {"left": {"title": "Flexbox: one dimension", "lang": "css", "code": ".toolbar {\n display: flex;\n justify-content: space-between;\n align-items: center;\n}", "note": "Content decides the size: navbars, toolbars, button rows."}, "right": {"title": "Grid: two dimensions", "lang": "css", "code": ".cards {\n display: grid;\n grid-template-columns:\n repeat(auto-fit, minmax(16rem, 1fr));\n gap: 1rem;\n}", "note": "The layout decides the size: page layouts, card galleries."}} ~~~ > **One dimension → Flexbox. Two dimensions → Grid.** If you are creating a navigation menu, button group, toolbar, or a row of controls, Flexbox is usually a natural choice. If you are creating a dashboard, photo gallery, or structured page with rows and columns, Grid is usually a better starting point. This does not mean you must choose one technology for an entire page. In fact, using both is normal. For example: ~~~text Page ├── Header → Flexbox │ ├── Logo │ └── Navigation → Flexbox │ ├── Main → Grid │ ├── Card │ ├── Card │ └── Card │ └── Card contents → Flexbox ├── Title └── Button ~~~ The outer page might use Grid while individual components use Flexbox. --- ## Centring an element both ways One of the most common CSS questions is: how do I put something exactly in the middle? With Flexbox: ~~~css .container { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; } ~~~ With a fixed-height container, this centres the child horizontally and vertically. Grid has an equally simple option: ~~~css .container { display: grid; place-items: center; } ~~~ `place-items: center` is a convenient shorthand for centring items on both axes. --- ## Using DevTools to understand layout Browser DevTools can make Flexbox and Grid much easier to learn. When you inspect a Flexbox container, modern browsers can show an overlay illustrating the container, axes, alignment, and spacing. You can turn this on from the Elements panel when the browser identifies a Flexbox container. Grid has a similar overlay. It can show grid lines, column and row boundaries, gaps, and named areas. This is much better than guessing. If a card is unexpectedly wide, inspect the parent. If items are not aligned, check the container's `flex-direction`, `justify-content`, and `align-items`. If a Grid layout has an unexpected number of columns, inspect `grid-template-columns`. DevTools is not just a debugging tool. It is also a learning tool. Change a value temporarily and immediately see what it does. --- ## The bigger picture Flexbox and Grid solve a major part of everyday frontend development: arranging components reliably across different screen sizes. You do not need dozens of CSS tricks. Start by identifying the relationship between the elements. Ask yourself: 1. Are these items mainly arranged in one direction? 2. Do I need rows and columns at the same time? 3. Should the items wrap? 4. Do I need consistent spacing? 5. Should the layout adapt automatically to the available width? If the answer points to one dimension, start with Flexbox. If the design is fundamentally a two-dimensional structure, start with Grid. Once you understand these two systems, many layouts that previously looked complicated become a small collection of predictable CSS rules.
takeaways: Flexbox is designed primarily for arranging items along one dimension, while Grid handles rows and columns together.
In Flexbox, justify-content works along the main axis and align-items works along the cross axis.
Grid's fr, repeat(), minmax(), and auto-fit functions make responsive layouts much easier to build.
Flexbox and Grid are complementary tools, and using Flexbox inside Grid-based components is completely normal.
Browser DevTools provides visual overlays that help you understand and debug both Flexbox and Grid layouts.

quiz.question: Which CSS property turns an element into a Flexbox container?
quiz.explanation: The display property creates the Flexbox formatting context. The direct children then become flex items.

quiz.question: With flex-direction: row, which property normally controls the vertical alignment of flex items?
quiz.explanation: With a horizontal row, the main axis is horizontal and the cross axis is vertical. align-items controls alignment on the cross axis.

quiz.question: What does repeat(3, 1fr) mean in grid-template-columns?
options: Create three rows that are each 1px wide
Repeat the entire grid three times
Create one column that is three fractions wide
quiz.explanation: repeat() avoids repeating the same declaration, so repeat(3, 1fr) creates three columns that each receive one flexible fraction.

quiz.question: Which pattern is particularly useful for an automatically responsive card grid without writing multiple media queries?
quiz.explanation: auto-fit combined with minmax() allows the browser to determine how many columns fit while maintaining a useful minimum column size.

quiz.question: Which tool can visually display Flexbox axes and Grid lines while you inspect a page?
quiz.explanation: Modern browser DevTools can display visual overlays for both Flexbox and Grid, making alignment, gaps, and tracks easier to understand.

exercise.title: Build a Flexbox header and Grid gallery
exercise.task: Create a complete HTML page containing the provided header and gallery structure, then use CSS to turn the header into a Flexbox layout and the gallery into a three-column Grid layout. The header must use Flexbox to place the logo and navigation on opposite sides and vertically centre them. The navigation must itself use Flexbox with visible spacing between its three links. The gallery must use exactly three equal columns with a visible gap, so the first three tiles appear on the first row and the remaining three appear on the second row. Use the exact class names `.logo`, `.menu`, `.gallery`, and `.tile` because the automated tests use them.
